newsitem.title: USA: White House panel set for digital TV obligations.
newsitem.headline: White House panel set for digital TV obligations.

text.p: President Clinton will create a panel to recommend whether to expand the public interest obligations of TV stations once they begin high-definition digital broadcasts, Vice President Al Gore said Wednesday.
The advisory group, which has yet to be named, will report to the president within a year on what obligation TV stations should have to the public in the coming digital age.
Existing ones include: three hours of educational TV for kids; discounted advertising rates for political candidates running for federal office; and equal TV time for candidates.
Once he receives the group's report, the president will then issue his own recommendations. The Federal Communications Commission, however, will have the final say in the matter.
Digital TV promises crystal-clear pictures and CD-quality sound. Industry officials say the broadcasts could begin to be on the air on a commercial basis by the end of 1998.
The digital system -- based on ones and zeroes of computer coding -- also will permit TV stations to broadcast up to five programmes of "standard" resolution simultaneously.
"Digital technology will greatly enhance the opportunities available to broadcasters to utilize multiple channels or programmes," Gore told a group of reporters.
"The public interest obligations should be commensurate with these new opportunities."
The White House will ask the FCC to hold off on making any final rules on the obligations for digital TV broadcasters while the advisory panel considers the issue.
But the administration will ask the FCC to proceed "expeditiously" with the allocation process for digital licenses, scheduled to begin in April, Gore said.
As a condition for receiving their broadcast licenses, TV stations are under obligation to provide certain services.
Greg Simon, an aide to Gore, told reporters the existing obligations will be carried forward into the digital age. He declined to offer examples of what changes could be made.
Advocates of campaign reform have suggested making free ad time for presidential candidates a public obligation.

"We are pleased the vice president has encouraged the FCC to proceed expeditiously with digital license allocations, and we look forward to reviewing the details of the special advisory group as that information becomes available," said Edward Fritts, chief executive of the National Association of Broadcasters.
